title: Down in the Valley
full_review:
The titular "valley" is not the iconic Western terrain you might imagine, but none other than Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley, and the Old West allusion is strictly intentional.

For "Down in the Valley" (THINKFilm) is an offbeat but quite interesting story about an easygoing South Dakota ranch hand named Harlan (an impressive Edward Norton), who romances October (Evan Rachel Wood) -- "Tobe" for short -- the rebellious (and much younger) teenage daughter of single father Wade, a correctional officer (David Morse). He also befriends her shy and emotionally fragile younger brother, Lonnie (Rory Culkin), who is clingingly attached to his big sister.

It's love at first sight for Tobe and Harlan when she and her friends stop for gas en route to the beach, and attendant Harlan fills their tank. On Tobe's invitation, he quits his job on the spot and joins the girls' outing.

Harlan's Western charm wins over Tobe, and they commence a physical relationship. Their bond deepens when she sees how thoughtful the gentle cowpoke is with Lonnie. Though he's probably twice her age, Harlan seems as innocent as she does, perhaps more so.

When Tobe takes Harlan out on the town for a night of barhopping, it is she who gives him recreational drugs, making you fear that she might be corrupting the unworldly man.

But wait a minute. Back at his lodgings, we see Harlan role-playing a prototypical gunslinger in front of his mirror. What's this all about? Is Harlan really the level-headed guy he appears to be? Something seems off-kilter.

The viewer is kept wondering about this character dichotomy, while Wade -- who demonstrates an increasing aversion to Harlan -- comes across as the bad guy, forbidding Harlan to date his daughter or see his son. Tobe, we have seen, has a grudge against her dad's occasional relationships with women, and there are several father-daughter spats that are quite ugly, with the expletives flying fast and furiously.

It's not spoiling anything to say that writer-director David Jacobson's initial "young lovers" romance shifts tone dramatically midway with a shocking twist, and ultimately becomes a suspenseful drama that pays homage to elements from the classic Westerns of John Ford and Howard Hawks.

The performances are solid across the board, with Norton (who co-produced) especially charismatic in a tricky role, and there's a good turn by Bruce Dern as an old codger whose horse Harlan "borrows" to impress Tobe.

The deconstruction of the mythic cowboy seems Jacobson's main thrust, with Lonnie's adulation of Harlan bringing to mind images of "Shane," to name one example. Though the film doesn't entirely avoid the feel of contrivance in its plotting, on the whole the film is more successful than not.

There are some violent episodes, but they are dispatched quickly with little gore, and though there are a couple of sexual encounters between Harlan and Tobe they're handled discreetly without nudity. The language used by these characters is quite strong, though, and may be a turnoff to many viewers.

This film contains considerable profanity, rough language and crude expressions, a couple of shootings, gun use by a minor, intense domestic discord, premarital sex and nongraphic sexual encounters, and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
